title: Scaling & Autoscaling Data Workloads on Kubernetes

scenes.heading: Scaling & Autoscaling on Kubernetes
scenes.narration: Autoscaling lets your data workloads grow and shrink automatically so capacity always matches demand without manual intervention.

scenes.heading: Kinds of scaling
bullets: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds or removes pods
Vertical Pod Autoscaler right-sizes CPU and memory
Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes nodes
Event-driven scaling with KEDA on queue depth
scenes.narration: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds or removes pod replicas based on load. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler right-sizes the CPU and memory requests of individual pods. The Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes whole nodes when pods cannot be scheduled or nodes sit idle. And KEDA enables event-driven scaling, reacting to signals like the depth of a message queue, which fits data pipelines especially well.

scenes.heading: Horizontal vs vertical scaling
scenes.narration: Horizontal scaling adds more replicas and shines for parallelizable work like processing many partitions, and adding pods causes no disruption. Vertical scaling instead makes each pod bigger, which suits memory-heavy single jobs, but resizing a running pod usually requires a restart. Most data platforms lean on horizontal scaling with vertical tuning where needed.

scenes.heading: A HorizontalPodAutoscaler
scenes.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: etl-worker
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: etl-worker
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
scenes.narration: This autoscaler targets the ETL worker deployment. It keeps at least two replicas for baseline availability and allows up to twenty at peak load. It scales based on CPU utilization, aiming to keep average usage around seventy percent. When utilization climbs above that target it adds pods, and when it drops it removes them, all automatically.

scenes.heading: The autoscaling loop
scenes.narration: The autoscaling loop continuously measures a metric such as CPU or queue depth. It compares that measurement against the target you set. Based on the difference it scales the number of pods up or down. If new pods cannot fit, the Cluster Autoscaler steps in to add nodes, and it removes nodes again once demand subsides.

scenes.text: Set sensible requests, choose the right autoscaler, and cap min and max so workloads scale efficiently and safely.
scenes.narration: Set sensible resource requests, choose the autoscaler that matches your workload, and always bound the minimum and maximum so your data workloads scale both efficiently and safely.
